title: Inference Infrastructure: Compact Narrative (Draft)
body:
Purpose and intent:
This is a compact, sales-and-ops-friendly narrative that explains why teams should treat inference as infrastructure and why Redwood is the practical choice. It is written to be dropped into battle cards, slide decks, and SDR scripts. The tone is pragmatic, engineering-centric, and focused on production economics and predictable outcomes.

Mission (one line):
Make inference dependable, predictable, and cost-efficient so engineering teams can ship LLM features without building a bespoke serving stack.

Thesis (short):
As models proliferate and hardware evolves, advantage shifts from model ownership to who can reliably deliver user-facing inference — with consistent latency, controllable unit cost, and operational guardrails. Teams win by standardizing on a serving layer that provides deployment parity, measurable economics, and graceful fallbacks.

Why treat inference as infrastructure? (2–3 bullets)
- Latency and cost are first-order product features: unpredictable tails or token cost spikes directly impact retention and CAC.
- Model variability is constant: teams need a runtime that can swap, quantize, or route models without user-visible regressions.
- Operational contracts matter: SLAs, auditability, key management, and safe rollouts are table stakes for production.

Why Redwood (core differentiators):
- Deployment parity: same API, rollout primitives, and observability across hosted, dedicated, and private modes — no forked engineering paths when you outgrow the sandbox.
- Cost-aware serving: autoscaled reserved capacity, intelligent batching/caching, and model quantization patterns that show up as predictable unit-economics improvements, not vague promises.
- Operational-first runtime: GPU-optimized kernels, KV cache management, and automatic fallbacks that preserve availability during noisy loads or degraded models.
- Developer ergonomics for production: clear metrics (per-route cost/latency), prompt-set driven quality checks, and fast SDKs so teams ship features rather than infra.

Proof points (what sales should cite):
- Engineering parity: customers move from POC to production with the same API and see median latency improvements and 20–40% token cost reduction via batching and caching suggestions.
- Reliability: automatic fallback to compatible model variants reduces outage surface during capacity events; customers report fewer incident escalations for inference.
- Security and compliance: support for customer-managed VPCs, KMS integrations, and audit logs required by regulated customers.

Target audiences (how to frame it):
- Early-stage AI-native startups: pitch speed to value + predictable unit economics (focus: self-serve API and quick rollout templates).
- Platform/infra teams at larger companies: pitch deployment parity and governance (focus: dedicated capacity, private deployments, rollouts).
- Product teams at mid-market/enterprise: pitch SLO-driven user experience and cost transparency (focus: console, per-route insights, and SLAs).

Key messaging primitives (short lines for use in copy):
- "Same API from sandbox to production — keep your code, change the capacity."
- "Turn model complexity into predictable economics."
- "Fallbacks, rollouts, and observability built for inference at scale."
- "Ship features, not infrastructure."

Dos and don’ts for reps and content authors:
- Do lead with operational outcomes (latency, cost, availability), not raw benchmark numbers.
- Do use customer stories that highlight a migration path (POC → Dedicated → Private).
- Don’t over-claim model performance superiority; focus on serving guarantees and developer velocity.
- Don’t bury the costs: be explicit about tradeoffs between latency targets, autoscaling policies, and unit economics.

Competitive positioning notes (short):
- Versus managed cloud endpoints: emphasize developer tooling, unified runtime, and predictable economics — not just raw access to GPUs.
- Versus model-access-only APIs: emphasize operational SLAs, private deployment options, and downgrade/fallback strategies.
- Versus self-hosted inference stacks: emphasize time-to-production, ongoing ops burden reduction, and smart autoscaling tuned to inference workloads.

Common objections and rebuttals (cheat sheet):
- "We can host cheaper ourselves." → Rebuttal: raw infra cost ignores engineering time, reliability incidents, and missed product velocity; we reduce those recurring hidden costs. Offer a TCO comparison template.
- "We need full control / air-gapped." → Rebuttal: Redwood Private offers customer-managed control plane and on-prem options with the same API surface so you keep control without rebuilding rollout and observability tooling.
- "Latency spikes are unacceptable." → Rebuttal: show per-route SLA options, edge/region routing, autoscale and caching knobs; propose a pilot with SLOs and trace-based baseline.

Two-line elevator pitches (audience-tuned):
- Technical lead: "Redwood gives you a serving runtime and ops toolkit so your team can deliver inference features with predictable latency and token economics — the same API whether you're on hosted, reserved, or private infrastructure."
- Head of product/ops: "We make inference a repeatable, measurable part of your product stack — fewer surprises on latency, cost, and rollouts, and fewer fire-drills for your engineering teams."

Suggested one-page slide layout (for short decks):
1) Problem: models change, infra is brittle, and cost/latency surprises break features.
2) Thesis: serving is the differentiator — you need predictable inference infrastructure.
3) Redwood solution: deployment parity, cost-aware serving, operational-first runtime.
4) Proof points: latency/cost wins, reliability anecdotes, security options.
5) Ask: pilot with defined SLOs and a migration plan.

Quick pilot template (sales-ready):
- Scope: 2 routes, 1 production model, 1 high-priority user flow.
- Success metrics: median latency target, 95th percentile SLO, and per-token cost improvement.
- Duration: 4–8 weeks with weekly checkpoints.

Open questions / follow up work for GtM: (notes for product marketing and GTM ops)
- Build a short TCO model that accounts for developer time, incidents, and infra ops — not just raw GPU cost.
- Capture three short customer migration stories (quantified improvements) for one-pager use.
- Create a pilot SOW template with clear SLOs and rollback policies.

Bottom line (one sentence):
Redwood turns inference into infrastructure you can depend on — reducing operational risk, clarifying unit economics, and letting engineering teams ship LLM-powered features faster.

(End of draft — trimming suggested for slide decks)
